title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budget policy, capacity planning, incident review standards, reliability initiatives, operational tooling recommendations, and runbook templates. It is intended for on-call engineers, service owners, and platform teams responsible for availability, latency, and cost targets of production inference services.

Goals
- Provide a consistent, measurable SLO framework across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Define a clear error-budget policy and escalation path to protect customer SLAs while enabling feature velocity.
- Standardize capacity planning and scaling guidance for GPU-backed inference services.
- Document incident review and postmortem standards to drive continuous reliability improvements.
- Provide runbook templates and recommended observability/operational tooling.

1) SLO definitions and measurement

1.1 SLO taxonomy
- Availability SLO (user-facing success rate): proportion of successful API responses (2xx) over total requests, measured monthly.
- Latency SLOs: p50, p95, p99 for request-to-first-byte (TTFB) or request-to-last-byte depending on route.
- Throughput/Capacity SLO: % of requests served within target concurrency/backlog thresholds.
- Correctness/Quality SLO (optional): model-quality checks for batched/critical customers (measured by evaluation harness).

1.2 Standard SLO targets (default baseline)
- Hosted API - Availability: 99.95% monthly (error budget 0.05% ~ 21.6 minutes/month).
- Hosted API - Latency: p95 <= 200ms for text-generation-short routes (<= 512 tokens).
- Dedicated pools - Availability: 99.9% monthly (error budget ~43.2 minutes/month).
- Embeddings service - Availability: 99.99% monthly for low-latency embedding routes.

Service owners may define stricter SLOs for high-tier customers; any deviation from the baseline must be documented in the service's Confluence page and approved by platform SRE.

1.3 Measurement strategy
- SLO windows: rolling 28-day and calendar-month views (both required).
- Error definition: a request is considered failed if response status is 5xx, 4xx configured-as-error (authorization/timeouts), or latency exceeds the defined per-route threshold.
- Signals: metrics (Prometheus), traces (Jaeger), logging (ELK), and synthetic checks (external probes).
- Example PromQL for availability (per-service):
  - "(sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=\"svc-name\",code=~\"2..\"}[30m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=\"svc-name\"}[30m])))"
- Example latency query (p95) using histogram_quantile:
  - "histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{service=\"svc-name\"}[5m])) by (le))"

2) Error budget policy and escalation

2.1 Error budget concepts
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. It represents how much unreliability is tolerated without requiring feature freezes or remediation.
- Burn rate = error budget consumed per unit time. We use a 7-day burn rate in addition to monthly windows for reactive control.

2.2 Burn policy and thresholds
- Green: burn rate <= 1 — standard operations, normal deployment cadence.
- Yellow (moderate): burn rate > 1 and <= 4 — reduce non-essential releases; inform stakeholders; increase monitoring cadence.
- Red (severe): burn rate > 4 — freeze feature rollouts for the affected service, prioritize mitigations, and escalate to Platform SRE.
- Continuous red for > 24 hours triggers an incident review and a postmortem.

2.3 Escalation steps (when error budget is in Yellow/Red)
1. Paginated alert to on-call SRE with incident context including affected SLO, burn rate, recent deploys, and relevant runbooks.
2. Owner (service/feature lead) presentation within 4 hours to SRE rotation.
3. Short-term mitigations: rollback recent deploys, increase autoscaling headroom, route traffic to fallback variants, and increase redundancy across regions.
4. If Red persists > 6 hours, create a reliability ticket with remediation timeline and assign to an owner.

3) Capacity planning and scaling guidance

3.1 Principles
- Plan for predictable tail latency under expected load while minimizing wasted GPU cycles.
- Use percentile-based sizing (p95/p99) for provisioning, not mean load.
- Model placement and packing: prefer GPU sharing for small models, dedicated GPUs for large low-latency models.
- Maintain a safety buffer (headroom) to handle sudden spikes and failovers.

3.2 Capacity Sizing process
1. Estimate baseline QPS and token generation rate per route using production telemetry.
2. Characterize workload: sequence length distribution, batchability, and KV-cache hit rates.
3. Measure per-request GPU utilization and latency at target batch sizes with the runtime perf-suite.
4. Calculate required GPUs = ceil((expected tokens/sec * avg_gpu_time_per_token) / gpu_seconds_per_gpu).
5. Add headroom: +25% for baseline, +50% for high-risk services or SLA-backed customers.

3.3 Autoscaling and policies
- Use a hybrid autoscaling model: reactive (CPU/GPU utilization and queue depth) + predictive (scheduled scaling from expected traffic patterns).
- Queue depth thresholds: trigger scale-up at queue depth > 50 requests for short-latency routes; scale-down when queue depth < 10 for > 10 minutes.
- Burst capacity: reserve a small pool of warm instances (1–2 instances per region) for cold-start sensitive models.

3.4 Capacity runbook checklist (pre-deploy)
- Confirm baseline SLO targets and error budget status.
- Run loadtest with representative prompt sets (use eval-harness).
- Verify KV cache warming strategy and expected cache hit rate.
- Confirm autoscaler policies and cooldown windows.

4) Incident review and postmortem standards

4.1 Scope and objectives
- All Sev2/Sev1 incidents and any continuous SLO breach lasting >24 hours require a postmortem.
- Objective: identify root cause, corrective actions, timeline of events, and follow-up tasks with owners and deadlines.

4.2 Postmortem template (required sections)
- Summary: brief incident description and customer impact.
- Timeline: ordered events with timestamps.
- Impact: SLOs affected, error budget consumed, customer-facing effects.
- Root cause analysis: technical and process contributors.
- Mitigations: immediate fixes performed during incident.
- Long-term actions: prioritized action items with owners and ETA.
- Lessons learned and follow-up review date.

4.3 Blamelessness and review process
- Postmortems must be blameless and focus on systemic fixes.
- Affected teams must present the postmortem at the weekly reliability sync within two weeks.
- Action items tracked in the reliability board and reviewed in SLO/ER reviews monthly.

5) Reliability initiatives and prioritization

5.1 Initiative types
- Infrastructure: GPU firmware/driver rollouts, kernel optimizations, multi-region redundancy.
- Observability: synthetic checks, SLO dashboards, latency histograms, headroom alerts.
- Process: runbook improvements, incident playbooks, error-budget governance.
- Quality: model regression tests and evaluation harness integration with CI.

5.2 Prioritization framework
- Initiatives ranked by expected SLO impact, cost, and implementation effort.
- Use RICE-style scoring (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort) for multi-team prioritization.
- Small, high-confidence reliability fixes should be fast-tracked; large initiatives require a proposal and roadmap slot.

6) Operational tooling and observability recommendations

6.1 Required tooling
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos for long-term retention.
- Tracing: Jaeger with sampling policy tuned for production (tail-sampling for errors).
- Logs: structured logging to ELK/Opensearch with message schemas.
- Synthetic checks: externally-run uptime and latency probes (every 30s for critical routes).
- Incident management: PagerDuty for on-call, Jira for reliability actions, Statuspage for customer comms.

6.2 Dashboards and alerts
- Per-service SLO dashboard: availability, latency percentiles, error budget burn, active incidents, deploy history.
- Alert categories: paging (sev1/sev2), notification (investigate), noise-suppressed (informational).
- Example paging alert: "Service SLO burn rate > 4 AND availability < 99.8% in last 30m".

6.3 Tooling integrations
- CI integration: run eval-harness tests and regression checks on canary releases; fail canaries on quality regression.
- Autoscaler integration: expose queue depth and headroom metrics to the autoscaler controller.
- Runbook linking: alerts should include direct link to the most recent runbook and postmortem.

7) Runbooks: template and examples

7.1 Runbook structure (required fields)
- Title
- Owner and on-call role
- Service(s) impacted and links to architecture diagrams
- Symptoms that should trigger the runbook (exact alert names/queries)
- Immediate mitigation steps (ordered)
- Diagnostics commands and queries (PromQL, CLI, logs)
- Rollback/restore steps and safety checks
- Post-incident actions and link to postmortem template

7.2 Example runbook: High P95 latency on text-generation-inference
- Symptom: p95 latency > 300ms for 10m, or queue depth > 75. Alert: "gen-service-p95-latency-high"
- Immediate steps:
  1. Acknowledge alert and notify service owner.
  2. Check recent deploys: `git log --max-count=5 --pretty=oneline` for the deployment tag.
  3. Inspect metrics: run p95 query and identify time of spike.
  4. Check queue depth and GPU utilization: `sum(queue_depth) by (instance)` and `avg(gpu_utilization) by (instance)`.
  5. If GPU saturation: increase replicas or raise max_batch_size to reduce per-token overhead (short-term).
  6. If recent deploy suspected: rollback to previous stable canary.
  7. If KV cache cold-starts causing latency: warm cache with synthetic traffic; scale warm instances.
- Diagnostics snippets (PromQL):
  - `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{service=\"gen-service\"}[5m])) by (le))`
  - `sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=\"gen-service\",code!~\"2..\"}[5m])) by (code)`

7.3 Post-incident checklist
- Capture timeline and attach logs and trace links.
- Record actions taken and rationale.
- Open postmortem and assign owners to action items within 48 hours.
- Verify SLO returns to acceptable state and error budget trend stabilizes.

8) Governance and review cadence

- SLO review: quarterly SLO review with service owners, product, and platform SRE to adjust targets based on usage and customer SLAs.
- Error budget review: weekly review of services with high burn rates.
- Reliability program review: monthly review of prioritized initiatives and action item status.

9) Ownership and contacts
- Platform SRE (primary): on-call rotation via PagerDuty (team: platform-sre@redwood.example.com).
- Service owners: listed on each service Confluence page.
- Reliability lead: Priya Kapoor (owner for reliability initiatives).

Appendices
A. Glossary
- SLO: Service Level Objective.
- SLA: Service Level Agreement.
- Error budget: allowed failure fraction.
- Burn rate: speed at which error budget is consumed.

B. Example SLO dashboard widgets
- Availability sparkline (28d)
- Error budget burn rate gauge (1h, 7d)
- Latency heatmap (p50/p95/p99)
- Active incidents with severity and owner

C. Related docs and templates
- Link: confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template (use for all Sev1/Sev2 incidents).
- Link: confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning-playbook (detailed sizing workbook).

If you are a service owner and need help aligning SLOs or onboarding a new service into the SRE program, contact platform-sre@redwood.example.com or schedule time on the reliability office hours calendar.
